# Where to run the analysis {#sec-computing}

Sequencing data are big, and the tools in this book run from the command line.
You can follow everything here on **your own laptop**, a **lab
workstation**, or a **shared computing cluster**. This chapter explains the
differences, so you can pick what fits and recognise the cluster words
(*node*, *job*, *SLURM*) when you meet them.

## Choosing a computer

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  Q1{"What are you doing?"} -->|"learning with the<br/>practice data"| LAP["Laptop or workstation is fine<br/>(chr22 references on 8 GB RAM;<br/>full references need ~16 GB)"]
  Q1 -->|"a real experiment<br/>(tens of millions of reads per sample)"| Q2{"Access to a cluster?"}
  Q2 -->|yes| CL["Cluster: batch jobs,<br/>scratch space, pipelines<br/>such as bagPipes"]
  Q2 -->|no| WS["A workstation with lots of RAM and disk,<br/>or a cloud machine"]
```

| | Laptop | Workstation | Cluster |
|---|---|---|---|
| Good for | Learning, small tests, R analysis | One project at a time | Many samples, pipelines |
| Typical RAM | 8–32 GB | 64–256 GB | Many nodes, each with lots |
| Disk | Hundreds of GB | TBs | Large shared storage |
| How you run tools | Type commands | Type commands | Submit **jobs** to a scheduler |
| Software | conda | conda | conda or **modules** |

A rough sense of what real data need: one human RNA-seq sample (30 M read
pairs) is ~3–5 GB of `.fastq.gz`; aligning it needs ~8 GB RAM (HISAT2) or
~32 GB (STAR); a whole experiment's outputs can be tens to hundreds of GB.

## Operating system

The tools are built for **Linux** and **macOS**. On **Windows**, install
[WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install) (Windows Subsystem for
Linux), which gives you an Ubuntu terminal, and follow the Linux
instructions inside it.

## Getting the software: conda

Bioinformatics tools are easiest to install with **conda**, which puts them in
an isolated *environment* (no administrator rights needed, and versions don't
clash between projects).

1. Install [Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge), a minimal conda.
2. Create the environments for this book from the files in its repository:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/jpflores-13/omics-walkthru.git
   cd omics-walkthru
   conda env create -f envs/rnaseq-tools.yml     # FastQC, Trim Galore, Salmon, HISAT2, samtools, ...
   conda env create -f envs/rnaseq-r.yml         # R, DESeq2, tximport, tximeta (optional)
   ```
3. Turn it on in each new terminal:

   ```bash
   conda activate rnaseq-tools
   salmon --version
   ```

::: {.callout-note}
## Apple Silicon Macs (M1–M4)

Some bioconda tools have no native ARM build yet. If `conda env create` says a
package isn't available for `osx-arm64`, create the environment for Intel Macs
(it runs through Rosetta):

```bash
CONDA_SUBDIR=osx-64 conda env create -f envs/rnaseq-tools.yml
```
:::

## Clusters in five minutes

A **cluster** is many computers (**nodes**) that share one file system. You
log in to a **login node**, shared by everyone and meant only for light work
(editing, copying, submitting). The real work runs on **compute nodes**, which
you request from a **scheduler**. The most common scheduler is **SLURM**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  L["Your laptop"] -- ssh --> LN["Login node<br/>(light work only)"]
  LN -- "sbatch / srun" --> S["Scheduler (SLURM)"]
  S --> C1["Compute node"]
  S --> C2["Compute node"]
  S --> C3["Compute node"]
  C1 & C2 & C3 --- FS[("Shared storage<br/>home · scratch · project")]
  LN --- FS
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Don't run FastQC, Salmon, HISAT2 or anything else heavy on a login node. It
slows the node for everyone and the process may be killed. Use an interactive
job or `sbatch`.
:::

### Storage on a cluster

Clusters usually have three kinds of space. The names differ, but the roles
are the same:

| Kind | Typical name | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **Home** | `~` | Scripts, configs. Small, backed up |
| **Scratch** | `/scratch`, `/work` | Running pipelines. Large and fast, **not backed up, purged** |
| **Project / lab** | `/proj`, `/project`, `/groups` | Raw data and results you keep. Shared, backed up |

A good habit: keep raw FASTQs in project space, run in scratch, and copy the
results you want to keep back to project space.

### Software on a cluster: modules

Clusters often offer preinstalled software as **environment modules**.
Pipelines such as bagPipes load tools this way at the start of each step:

```bash
module avail salmon          # what versions exist?
module load salmon/1.10.3    # use this one
module list                  # what is loaded
module purge                 # unload everything
```

conda works on clusters too, and gives you the same versions as on your laptop.

### Running jobs with SLURM

**Interactive job**, to work on a compute node by hand:

```bash
srun -n 1 -c 4 --mem=8g -t 2:00:00 --pty bash      # add -p <partition> if your cluster needs one
```

**Batch job**, for real runs. Write a script with `#SBATCH` lines saying
what you need, then submit it:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J my_job           # job name
#SBATCH -t 4:00:00          # time limit
#SBATCH -c 4                # CPUs
#SBATCH --mem=16g           # memory
#SBATCH -o %x-%j.out        # log file: <jobname>-<jobid>.out
conda activate rnaseq-tools  # or: module load ...
salmon quant ...
```

```bash
sbatch my_job.sh            # submit
squeue -u $USER             # what's running / waiting?
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS   # how did it go?
scancel 123456              # cancel
```

Other schedulers (PBS, LSF, SGE) work the same way with different command
names (`qsub`, `bsub`, `qstat`).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## On UNC Longleaf (Phanstiel lab)

- Log in: `ssh <onyen>@longleaf.unc.edu`.
- Storage: home `/nas/longleaf/home/<onyen>`; scratch
  `/work/users/<first letter>/<second letter>/<onyen>` (purged); lab space
  `/proj/phanstiel_lab/`.
- Interactive jobs: `srun -p interact -n 1 --mem=8g -t 2:00:00 --pty bash`.
- Batch partition: `-p general`.
- Software: everything bagPipes needs is available as modules (`module avail`).
- Prebuilt references: `/proj/phanstiel_lab/Reference/human/hg38/` (see
  [Practice setup](practice-setup.qmd)).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. You want to look at the first read in a FASTQ file on a cluster. Is it OK
   on the login node?
2. Where should a 200 GB pipeline output go while it's being made?
3. You're on a Windows laptop. What do you install first?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. Yes. `zcat file.fastq.gz | head -4` is light work.
2. Scratch space: fast and large. Copy what you keep to project space after,
   because scratch is purged.
3. WSL, then Miniforge inside it.
:::
:::
